options.text: Set the old system to read-only now so the remaining planners have to move across, and handle any complaints through the service desk.
options.rationale: It forces the move the plan requires, but without knowing what the 35 are relying on. If one of them runs a process the new system cannot support, the cost lands on live operations.

options.text: Close the project on schedule and transfer the old system's decommissioning to IT operations as a business-as-usual task.
options.rationale: This hands over an unfinished scope item together with an unexplained adoption problem. Decommissioning was in the project's scope, and IT operations has no authority over planners' working practices.

options.text: Arrange refresher training on the new system for the 35 planners, since continued use of an old system usually reflects low confidence.
options.rationale: Training is a sensible response if confidence is the cause, but nothing here shows that it is. The candidate is acting on the common cause rather than the actual one.

questions.explanation: Retiring the system being replaced is often part of a project's scope, and the business case usually depends on it. When some users keep using the old system, that is a sign of an unmet need, a missing report or a workaround, and it has to be understood before the old system is removed. The switch-off date itself belongs to the business owner, and making it a dated item in the closure plan stops it drifting into operations unfinished.
questions.mindset: When people keep using the old way, find out what it still does for them before taking it away.

questions.stem: Over a year, an agile team has built 22 operational dashboards for a supermarket chain's supply-chain analysts. The team disbands in three weeks and a small business intelligence support team will take over. Usage logs show that six dashboards account for nearly all views and nine have not been opened in four months. Each dashboard handed over adds monitoring and data-refresh work for the support team. Which two actions should the delivery lead take?

options.text: Agree with the product owner which unused dashboards to retire, checking with the people who originally requested them, before preparing the handover.
options.rationale: Each dashboard handed over carries a support cost, and closure is the cheapest point to stop carrying the ones that are unused. Checking with the requesters catches dashboards used only at year end or for audits.

options.text: Include the usage figures in the closure report, so the benefits owner can see which parts of the product are actually delivering value.
options.rationale: Usage is the clearest evidence of value the team has. Putting it in the closure report gives the benefits owner and future funders an accurate picture instead of a count of features delivered.

options.text: Hand over all 22 dashboards, since each was accepted by the product owner and retiring them would throw away work the organisation has already paid for.
options.rationale: The money spent building the unused dashboards is gone whichever way the decision goes. Handing them over adds a running cost to protect a cost that cannot be recovered.

options.text: Spend the final sprints improving the nine unused dashboards so that analysts are more likely to adopt them after the team has left.
options.rationale: It invests the last of the team's time in the least proven part of the product, with nobody left afterwards to see whether adoption follows.

options.text: Hand over the six popular dashboards only and delete the other sixteen now, because the logs show that nobody is using them.
options.rationale: The direction is right but the decision is taken alone, and the logs cover only four months. Dashboards used quarterly or annually, and those between the two groups, would be lost without anyone being asked.

questions.explanation: A handover transfers running cost as well as value, and the receiving team pays for every feature it inherits. Closure is the natural point to retire what is not used, with the product owner's agreement and a check for infrequent use, and to report actual usage so that value is judged on evidence rather than on what was built. Money already spent is not a reason to keep spending.
questions.mindset: Hand over what earns its upkeep; retiring the rest is a delivery decision, not a loss.

questions.stem: You manage three equipment-installation contracts for different clients. Each contract requires the client to accept or reject the works in writing, with reasons, within 15 working days of the acceptance tests, and treats the works as accepted if the client does neither in that time. Match each situation to the closure response that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A print works has signed acceptance and attached a list of four cosmetic items, such as a scratched guard panel, none of which affects operation.
A dairy has neither accepted nor rejected the works, and 17 working days have passed since it witnessed the acceptance tests.
A brewery has rejected the works in writing because its new filling line ran at 82% of the contracted throughput during the tests.

options.text: Record the acceptance and agree dated completion of the listed items, tracked through to closure
options.rationale: The client has accepted. Minor items listed with an acceptance do not reopen it; they are finished against agreed dates and tracked so the contract can close cleanly.

options.text: Record deemed acceptance under the contract and notify the client of it in writing
options.rationale: The contract says what silence means, and the period has passed. Recording it and telling the client in writing makes the position clear without waiting indefinitely for a signature.

options.text: Correct the shortfall and repeat the relevant tests before seeking acceptance again
options.rationale: A written rejection against a contracted performance figure is valid. The work has not met its criterion, so it is put right and retested rather than argued over.

options.text: Treat the silence as rejection and arrange a full repeat of the acceptance tests
options.rationale: Not used. This reads the dairy's silence as a rejection, which is the opposite of what the contract says, and repeats testing nobody has challenged.

questions.explanation: Acceptance is a contractual event, and the contract defines how it happens: by signature, by deemed acceptance when the client neither accepts nor rejects in time, or not at all when a criterion is properly failed. Minor items attached to a signed acceptance are tracked to completion without reopening it, while a genuine failure against a contracted measure is remedied and retested. Reading each situation against the contract's mechanism keeps closure from depending on goodwill or impatience.
questions.mindset: Let the contract's acceptance terms, not the mood of the moment, decide when the work is accepted.

questions.stem: A concert hall's hybrid project, which replaced its stage lighting rig and built a new ticketing app in sprints, is closing. Your financial closure review finds three loose ends, all within your authority as budget holder. Match each one to the action that clears it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A purchase order for lighting-technician training still has an uncommitted £8,000 balance, because the supplier's course turned out not to be needed.
Two developers released to another project last month have carried on booking their time to this project's cost code.
The rigging supplier issued a £3,100 credit note for a late delivery, and its final invoice for £22,400 has arrived but is not yet paid.

options.text: Cancel the remaining commitment so the funds are released back to the budget
options.rationale: An open balance on an order nobody will use still reads as committed money. Cancelling it returns the funds and stops anyone raising an invoice against it later.

options.text: Have the bookings moved to the correct cost code and tell the other project's manager
options.rationale: The cost belongs to the project that used the time. Correcting it keeps both projects' actuals honest, and telling the other manager stops the error recurring.

options.text: Deduct the credit from the final invoice before approving it for payment
options.rationale: The final invoice is the last chance to recover the credit without chasing a supplier the project no longer deals with. Once paid in full, the credit tends to be forgotten.

options.text: Leave the item open on the cost code and note it for the year-end audit to resolve
options.rationale: Not used. Each loose end here can be cleared now by the budget holder. Leaving any of them for audit pushes the work onto people with less context and leaves the figures wrong until then.

questions.explanation: Financial closure means the project's books show only what the project actually committed and consumed. Uncommitted balances are released, costs booked to the wrong place are moved to where they belong, and money owed to the project is recovered before the final payment goes out. Where these sit within the budget holder's authority, they are cleared at closure rather than left for finance or audit to rebuild later from less information.
questions.mindset: Leave the books as you would want to inherit them: every commitment used, released or recovered.

questions.stem: An online travel agency's search-platform team disbands on Friday and its service passes to a support team on Monday. Complete each sentence with the action that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Three contract developers finish on Friday and still hold administrator access to production. Their accounts should be
The deployment pipeline uses a shared service-account password that every team member has seen. Before handover, that credential should be

options.text: removed on their last working day, with the removal confirmed in the access log
options.rationale: Access is granted for a need, and the need ends on Friday. Removing it then, and confirming it, closes a door that otherwise stays open with nobody watching it.

options.text: rotated, with the new value held only by the support team in the secrets vault
options.rationale: A secret known to people who are leaving should be treated as exposed. Rotating it at handover gives the support team sole control of the pipeline they now own.

options.text: left active for 30 days so the support team can call on them if something goes wrong
options.rationale: Not used. Knowledge can be kept available by agreement without leaving production access open. A grace period turns a convenience into an unmonitored risk.

questions.explanation: Access granted for a project should end when the project's need for it ends, and credentials known to people who are leaving should be treated as compromised. Both are closure tasks with a clear moment — the last working day and the handover — and missing that moment usually means nobody notices until an audit or an incident.
questions.mindset: Access should end when the need for it ends, not when someone remembers to remove it.

questions.stem: An agile supplier is paid €1,150 per accepted story point, up to a contract ceiling of €460,000. Before the final sprint, 371 points had been accepted and paid for. In the final sprint the team delivered 52 points, of which 41 were accepted and 11 rejected. The contract has now ended.

blanks.label: Total value of all accepted story points at the contract rate, in €
blanks.rationale: Accepted points are 371 + 41 = 412. At €1,150 each, 412 × 1,150 = €473,800. The 11 rejected points earn nothing.

blanks.label: Final payment due to the supplier, in €
blanks.rationale: Paid so far is 371 × 1,150 = €426,650. The ceiling caps total payment at €460,000, below the €473,800 earned, so the final payment is 460,000 − 426,650 = €33,350.

blanks.label: Value of accepted work that the ceiling leaves unpaid, in €
blanks.rationale: Accepted value above the ceiling is 473,800 − 460,000 = €13,800. Under the contract, this is work the supplier delivered at its own risk.

questions.explanation: Closing a unit-rate contract means applying every term that governs payment, not only the rate: only accepted units are payable, and a ceiling limits the total whatever is delivered. The final payment is the lower of the earned value and the ceiling, less what has already been paid. A ceiling moves the risk of over-delivery to the supplier, which is why both sides should track it sprint by sprint rather than discover it at closure.
questions.mindset: Close a contract by applying every term that limits payment, not only the rate.

questions.stem: A coastal path restoration project's closure board lists six items. The organisation's policy allows closure once every item is either complete or transferred to a named owner who has confirmed acceptance in writing. Select the item that prevents the project from closing.

graphic.title: Closure board listing six items with their status
graphic.caption: Select an item. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between items, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Client acceptance — signed by the national park's estates manager on 3 June
regions.rationale: Acceptance is signed by the client's named authority, so this item is complete and does not hold up closure.

regions.label: Benefits tracking — visitor counts transferred to the park's visitor services lead, accepted in writing
regions.rationale: Benefits are measured after closure by design. The item has a named owner who has accepted it in writing, which is exactly what the policy asks for.

regions.label: Two loose handrails — passed to the ranger team's maintenance list; acceptance confirmed in writing by the head ranger
regions.rationale: Open defects are allowed under this policy as long as someone has accepted them. The head ranger has, so the handrails are a transferred item rather than a blocker.

regions.label: Lessons learned — captured and submitted; the PMO publishes them next quarter
regions.rationale: The project's part is complete once the lessons are captured and submitted. Publishing them is the PMO's own process and does not keep the project open.

regions.label: Contractor warranty claims — passed to procurement; acceptance requested three weeks ago, no reply yet
regions.rationale: This item has been sent to procurement but not accepted by it. Until a named owner confirms in writing, the warranty claims still belong to the project, so the project cannot close.

regions.label: Project team — all eight members released to their line managers
regions.rationale: Release of the team is complete. It is a closure activity, not an outstanding condition.

questions.explanation: A project can close with work still outstanding, provided each open item has an owner who has agreed to take it. The test is acceptance by the receiver, not dispatch by the sender: an item sent but not accepted still belongs to the project. Items that are measured or published after closure by design, such as benefits and lessons, are not blockers once their owner has accepted them.
questions.mindset: An item is handed over when someone has accepted it, not when it has been sent.

questions.stem: An agile team has built an eSIM activation service for a mobile network operator and is due to be reassigned in three weeks. The site reliability team that will run the service has declined to sign the handover, saying only that it is 'not operable yet'. The product owner says every story met the definition of done, and the sponsor wants the handover signed this week. What should the delivery lead do first?

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor to direct the site reliability team to accept the service, since every story met the agreed definition of done.
options.rationale: The definition of done is a real agreement, but it may never have included what operators need. Escalating a vague objection forces a decision before anyone knows whether the objection is right.

options.text: Meet the site reliability lead to establish which specific operability criteria the service fails and what evidence would satisfy them.
options.rationale: 'Not operable' could mean a missing runbook or no alerting at all. Turning it into a list is the step that tells everyone whether to fix, fund or push back, and three weeks leaves time to act on the answer.

options.text: Plan two hardening sprints covering monitoring, alerting and runbooks, the usual operability gaps, and ask the sponsor to fund the extension.
options.rationale: These are the usual gaps, which makes this a reasonable guess. But it commits money and time to a cause nobody has confirmed, and may miss the actual concern.

options.text: Hand the service over this week with the delivery team on call for a month, so the site reliability team has support while concerns come out.
options.rationale: It gives support, but it moves the service to a team that has refused it without finding out why. The concern surfaces as an incident instead of as a requirement.

questions.explanation: A receiving team's refusal to accept a handover is a request for information, not a verdict to override or obey. The first step is to turn the objection into specific criteria and evidence, which then shows whether the gap is real work, a misunderstanding or an unreasonable demand. When the gap turns out to be operational requirements missing from the definition of done, that is also a lesson for how future teams agree it.
questions.mindset: Turn a vague 'not ready' into a specific list before deciding whether to fix, fund or push back.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project has installed 1,200 air-quality sensors across a city, with the public data dashboard built in sprints. The sensors' mobile data contracts were bought on the project's cost centre with you named as account holder, and they auto-renew for a year in seven weeks. The city's environmental health manager will run the network after closure next month and has a budget line for running costs. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Transfer the contracts' account ownership, billing and renewal to the environmental health manager, with her written acceptance, before closure.
options.rationale: She owns the service and has the budget. Moving the contracts into her name before the renewal means the obligation sits with the person who will run the network for its whole life.

options.text: Let the contracts auto-renew on the project cost centre, and ask finance to recharge the environmental health budget each month afterwards.
options.rationale: The service keeps running and the cost ends up in the right budget, but a closed project stays the account holder for a year. The candidate is solving the money and leaving the ownership where it was.

options.text: Give the environmental health manager the account login details and renewal date in the handover pack, so she can take over when she is ready.
options.rationale: Handing over information is not handing over the contract. The account, the renewal and the liability stay with the project until someone formally takes them on.

options.text: Renew the contracts for a year from the project's remaining budget before closure, so the sensors keep working while ownership is arranged.
options.rationale: It protects continuity, but spends project funds on a year of operations and postpones the transfer it is meant to enable.

questions.explanation: Anything the project holds in its own name that the product needs in order to keep running — contracts, accounts, licences, permits, subscriptions — has to be formally transferred to the operational owner before closure. Passing on information about it is not a transfer, and a closed project cannot meet an obligation that is still in its name. Renewal dates set the real deadline.
questions.mindset: If the project's name is on it and the product still needs it, it has to change hands before closure.
